## Proof

Define $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ where $x_1, \dots, x_n$ range independently over $[0,1]$, so that
$$f(n) = \int_{[0,1]^n} \exp\!\bigl(-1/S_n\bigr)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(-1/S_n)\bigr].$$

We extend the integrand to $S_n = 0$ by setting $\exp(-1/0) = \lim_{t\to 0^+} e^{-1/t} = 0$, which is consistent and harmless since $\{S_n = 0\}$ has measure zero.

**Key observation.** The map $g(t) = \exp(-1/t)$ for $t > 0$ (with $g(0)=0$) is **strictly increasing** on $[0,\infty)$, since
$$g'(t) = \frac{1}{t^2}\,e^{-1/t} > 0 \quad \text{for all } t > 0.$$

**Comparison.** Write $f(n+1)$ by isolating the last variable:
$$f(n+1) = \int_{[0,1]^n}\left[\int_0^1 \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n + x_{n+1}}\Bigr)\,dx_{n+1}\right]dx_1\cdots dx_n.$$

For every fixed $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in[0,1]^n$ and every $x_{n+1}\in[0,1]$:
$$S_n + x_{n+1} \;\geq\; S_n,$$
with strict inequality whenever $x_{n+1} > 0$. Since $g$ is strictly increasing,
$$\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n + x_{n+1}}\Bigr) \;\geq\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n}\Bigr),$$
strictly for $x_{n+1} > 0$ (on a set of full measure in $x_{n+1}$, for a.e.\ $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ with $S_n > 0$).

Integrating over $x_{n+1}\in[0,1]$:
$$\int_0^1 \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n + x_{n+1}}\Bigr)\,dx_{n+1} \;>\; \int_0^1 \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n}\Bigr)\,dx_{n+1} = \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{1}{S_n}\Bigr),$$
for almost every $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in[0,1]^n$ (those with $S_n>0$, i.e., a.e.).

Integrating over $[0,1]^n$:
$$f(n+1) \;>\; \int_{[0,1]^n} \exp(-1/S_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n \;=\; f(n).$$

**Conclusion.** $f(n+1) > f(n)$ for every $n \geq 1$, so $f(n)$ is **strictly increasing** in $n$.
